script: Everyone says the QWERTY keyboard was designed to slow typists down. That's not what happened. 1868, Milwaukee. Printer and inventor Christopher Latham Sholes patented one of the first practical typewriters, with Carlos Glidden and Samuel Soule. The first layout was alphabetical - A, B, C in order. It jammed constantly. Type fast, and the metal arms crossed and locked up. So Sholes rearranged the keys - not to slow anyone down, but to separate the letter pairs that jammed the machine most often. In 1873, he sold the rights to Remington for twelve thousand dollars. They marketed it as the Remington Typewriter, and QWERTY went out into the world. There's no evidence Sholes ever tried to handicap typists - and at the time, touch typing didn't even exist yet, so there was no one to sabotage. QWERTY stuck around for one simple reason: everyone already knew it. Changing it later would mean retraining an entire planet. A hundred and fifty years later, we're all still typing on a layout built to save a machine, not slow down a person. Follow for more true stories with a twist nobody expects.

metadata.title: Random But True: The QWERTY Myth Everyone Believes Is Wrong
metadata.caption:
The QWERTY keyboard was not designed to slow typists down. That story is a myth.

1868, Milwaukee. Christopher Latham Sholes patented one of the first practical typewriters. The first layout was alphabetical - and it jammed constantly, since frequently-typed adjacent letters made the metal typebars strike each other and lock up.

So Sholes rearranged the keys to separate the letter pairs that clashed most often. Not to slow anyone down - to keep the machine from breaking. In 1873 he sold the rights to Remington for $12,000, and QWERTY went out into the world as the Remington Typewriter.

There's no real evidence Sholes ever tried to handicap typists - touch typing didn't even exist yet, so there was no one fast enough to sabotage.

QWERTY stuck around for one reason: everyone already knew it. A century and a half later, we're all still typing on a layout built to save a machine, not slow down a person.

Follow for more true stories with a twist nobody expects.
